tagline: A colonial port’s ruins beneath the earthworks of a Confederate fort
intro: Brunswick Town Road appears among the Coastal Plain routes in North Carolina’s scenic-byways guide. Its historic setting is the Cape Fear River: Orton Plantation lies beside the river between Wilmington and Southport, and the ruins of Brunswick Town lie south of Orton. The town’s historic district contains colonial house ruins, St. Philip’s Church and Fort Anderson.

Brunswick became a busy port exporting tar, pitch and turpentine for naval and merchant ships. British forces burned most of its buildings in 1776. After a few families returned, the port continued functioning, but by 1830 the abandoned town site sold to Orton’s owner for $4.25.

From Orton, the geographic sequence runs south to Brunswick Town, where the church ruins and Fort Anderson occupy the same historic district. Confederate earthworks covered the remains of burned buildings; St. Philip’s Church was left uncovered. Outdoor trails lead past the excavated fort and town ruins.

moments.title: Orton Plantation
moments.text: Orton’s rice plantation was developed through the unpaid labor of hundreds of enslaved people. The house began as a one-and-a-half-story white brick building; a second floor and four fluted Doric columns were added in 1840. After the Confederate defeat at Fort Fisher, Union soldiers took the property and used the house as a military hospital, sparing it from destruction. Public garden visits began as a fundraiser after a relative of the Sprunt family was injured in a car accident. The gardens and chapel later became a public attraction, but that chapter ended with the plantation’s sale in 2010.

moments.title: St. Philip's Church
moments.text: Four brick walls survive at St. Philip’s, where fire destroyed the roof, floor, doors and windows. Construction began in 1754 and finished in 1768, only eight years before British forces burned the church during the Revolutionary War. Confederate engineers later built defenses through the town’s ruins, leaving the church uncovered. Union naval cannonballs struck its walls during the February 1865 attack on Fort Anderson. The masonry is three feet thick, built with bricks imported from England. Excavations beginning in 1958 recovered bullets, buttons and a cannonball from inside the church ruins.
moments.notice: Cannonball strikes remain visible on the church walls.

moments.title: Fort Anderson
moments.text: Fort Anderson placed a Confederate river defense over the remains of a colonial port. Its earthen batteries supported and shielded cannon, while shelters beneath some earthworks protected troops during bombardment. The fort was intended to obstruct Union ships and protect Wilmington’s supply route against the blockade. Archaeological work later recovered streets and house foundations beneath this military landscape. The visitor center interprets both periods, and outdoor trails pass the excavated ruins of the town and fort. Originally called Fort St. Philip after the nearby church, the fort was renamed to honor Colonel George B. Anderson.

practical: Orton Plantation: The plantation and grounds are closed to the general public following the 2010 sale. (checked 2026-10-11)
